raw_response:
I farm about 20 mu here in Quzhou County, and I've learned over the years that sticking with what this land does best is smarter than chasing fancy crops. I'm going with the wheat–maize double cropping system on all 20 mu. Wheat is already in the ground from last October — I sowed an improved semi-dwarf variety that handles our winters well and responds to fertilizer. Come June, the day after harvest, I'll plant hybrid maize. I never save maize seed; the hybrid vigor is worth every yuan, and I buy Nongda 372 or something similar from the county supply store.

For fertilizer, I think in terms of target yield. I'm aiming for about 500 kg per mu of wheat and roughly 550–600 kg per mu of maize. To get there, I apply a compound fertilizer base before wheat planting — about 50 kg per mu of 15-15-15 compound, which gives me a solid foundation of N, P, and K. Then at wheat jointing in mid-March, I topdress with urea, about 20 kg per mu. For maize, I band compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress urea at the V6 stage. All told, that works out to about 16 kg of pure nitrogen per mu for wheat and 15 kg for maize, with modest phosphorus and potassium to keep the soil balanced. I know some neighbors skip the P and K, but I've seen the yield drag after a few years of that, so I keep it in the program.

Irrigation is from our tube well, and electricity isn't cheap, but going dry at jointing or tasseling is false economy. I irrigate wheat four times — green-up, jointing, booting, and grain filling. For maize, I aim for two times: one right after planting if the soil is dry, and one at tasseling in late July or early August when the heat hits hardest.

Pest control is preventive. I spray herbicide once on each crop — wheat gets a broadleaf herbicide in early spring, maize gets a pre-emergence treatment. Insecticide goes on twice for wheat against aphids and twice for maize against stem borer. I keep one fungicide application ready for wheat if the spring turns humid; I watch the weather and decide at flag leaf.

Tillage-wise, I rotary-tilled before wheat planting last fall. For maize, there's no time — wheat comes off in early June and maize has to be in the ground within days, so I plant no-till directly into the wheat stubble with my no-till seeder. The residue helps keep moisture in during July.
